newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM keeps markets guessing on new finance chief.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM keeps markets guessing on new finance chief.

text.p: Thailand's premier kept financial markets guessing on Thursday as to who his new finance minister would be ahead of an appointment to be made on Friday.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh told a news conference that he had "a long list" of strong candidates and expected to reach a decision on Thursday night to ensure a quick appointment.
Government sources and analysts told Reuters that Chavalit's list of candidates for the job ranged from a coterie of eminent bankers to former ministers. But the job would be tough.
Chavalit stressed that his new finance minister would not be a politician. "The public tend not to trust politicians for this portfolio. Therefore, we will opt for a competent outsider," he said.

Amnuay was a non-elected member of the cabinet. He quit because of political differences with rivals in the six-party coalition government over his management of the troubled economy which is in its worst slump in over a decade.
Thailand has seen five finance ministers in three governments since 1995.

Among the prospective candidates was deputy central bank governor Chaiwat Wibulsawasdi who used to be caretaker finance minister in a caretaker government from October-November 1996. Olarn Chaiprawat, the top executive of leading Siam Commercial Bank, was also mentioned as another possible replacement for Amnuay. But sources close to him said Olarn had expressed no interest and was on a business trip to Germany.
Another strong candidate for the job was Virapongsa Ramangura, a former deputy finance minister and economic adviser to powerful Prime Minister Prem Tinsulanonda during the 1980s, the sources said.
There was also speculation that the chief of state-run Exim Bank, Pridiyathorn Devakul, and former top banker and communications minister, Vichit Surapongchai, had also been approached.
But Pridiyathorn denied the talk, saying he had never been approached nor did he think he was ready for the job.
Vichit, a former top executive of Thailand's largest Bangkok Bank, could not be reached for comment.
Analysts said it would be difficult for this government to find a choice that could emulate Amnuay, who was a successful banker and a technocrat before entering politics.

"I don't see at the moment a strong candidate available to really take control of the situation given the political constraints in the cabinet. My suggestion to government and the authority is to seek advice from the IMF," said Graham Catterwell, managing director of Deutsche Morgan Grenfrell.

Khanchit Assavasamran of Vickers Ballas said the portfolio was an unenviable job as the new finance minister would have to handle the troubled economy and political infighting in the ruling six-party coalition.

"There are two key issues for the economy -- growth and stability. Amnuay has done well in his efforts to achieve stability but that came at the expense of growth which did not bode well for him," he said.

"A new finance minister might be a very capable man. But he cannot move anything forward without cooperation from politicians. Amnuay is a good example to show that it is not easy to do that,' he added.
